standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: ResponseEntity is your escape hatch from always returning 200 OK — it puts you in full control of the HTTP response.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: ResponseEntity is a return type that wraps the response body, status code, and headers into one object. When you return it from a @RestController method, Spring uses exactly what you put in it — no defaults applied.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Without ResponseEntity, every method returns 200 OK. That works for simple cases but breaks REST conventions — a POST that creates a resource should return 201, a DELETE should return 204, and a GET for a missing resource should return 404.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: ResponseEntity.ok(body): 200 OK with a response body — most common.
ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(saved): 201 Created with Location header and body.
ResponseEntity.noContent().build(): 204 No Content — nothing to return.
ResponseEntity.notFound().build(): 404 Not Found — resource doesn't exist.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: ResponseEntity.created(uri) does two things at once — sets the status to 201 and adds a Location header pointing to the new resource URL. REST best practice requires this for POST responses, but many fresher implementations return 200 and skip the Location header entirely.

cap: Chain Optional with ResponseEntity for clean conditional responses: optional.map(ResponseEntity::ok).orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build())

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: HTTP status codes are the language your API uses to tell clients what happened. Always returning 200 is like saying 'fine' to every question.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Status codes are grouped by their first digit. 2xx means success. 4xx means the client did something wrong. 5xx means something broke on the server.

beats.label: parts_or_states
rows: Successful GET, PUT, PATCH with body
DELETE or PUT/PATCH with no body
Not logged in or missing credentials

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: The 4xx vs 5xx distinction is important. A 4xx means the client made a mistake and should fix their request. A 5xx means the server has a problem. This distinction matters for alerting — 5xx errors are the ones that wake engineers up at night.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: 401 and 403 are often confused. 401 Unauthorized means the user isn't authenticated — they haven't proven who they are. 403 Forbidden means they're authenticated but they don't have permission to do this specific thing. Despite the name, 401 is really about authentication, not authorization.

cap: Always return 201 for POST and 204 for DELETE. Returning 200 for everything is technically functional but wrong — clients and monitoring tools depend on accurate codes.
followup_handoff: What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
Why should POST return 201 instead of 200?

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: ResponseEntity's builder chain lets you set status, headers, and body in one readable line — no manual HttpServletResponse needed.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: To add custom headers to a ResponseEntity, you create an HttpHeaders object, add your headers using the typed setter methods or the generic add method, and pass it to the builder chain with .headers().

beats.label: example
beats.content: The most important real-world use is the Location header for 201 Created responses. When you create a new resource, REST best practice says the response should tell the client where to find it. ResponseEntity.created(uri) sets both the 201 status and the Location header in one call.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Location: points to the newly created resource — headers.setLocation(uri) or shorthand ResponseEntity.created(uri).
Cache-Control: controls how long clients and proxies cache the response.
X-Request-ID: custom correlation header for distributed tracing.
Content-Type: usually auto-set by Spring — override only when needed.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: gotcha: Spring automatically sets Content-Type to application/json for @RestController responses. If you set it manually to a different value through headers but return a Java object, Spring may serialize it to JSON anyway and the Content-Type header won't match the actual body.

cap: For a proper 201 response: ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/api/users/" + saved.getId())).body(saved) — status, Location header, and body in one call.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: Conditional responses are where ResponseEntity really earns its place — different outcomes need different status codes.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: When the status code depends on runtime logic, ResponseEntity lets you build the right response in each branch. The cleanest approach chains Optional with ResponseEntity in a single expression.

beats.label: example
beats.content: The Optional map pattern is idiomatic Spring: findById returns an Optional, map transforms the found value into a 200 response, and orElse provides a 404 fallback. One line, no null checks.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: For more complex logic, use explicit if-else blocks. Check existence first, return 404 early, then proceed with the operation and return 200. This keeps the method readable.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: In large codebases, handling every possible response in every controller becomes repetitive. The better pattern is to throw custom exceptions from the service layer — UserNotFoundException, ResourceConflictException — and catch them in a @ControllerAdvice that maps each exception type to the right ResponseEntity. Your controllers stay clean and the error-to-status mapping lives in one place.

cap: Be consistent across your API — either use ResponseEntity in all endpoints, or use @ResponseStatus with exceptions. Mixing patterns makes the codebase harder to follow.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: @ResponseStatus and ResponseEntity both set HTTP status codes — but one decides at compile time and the other at runtime.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: @ResponseStatus is a static annotation. Whatever status code you set in the annotation is always returned, no matter what happens in the method body. It's a declaration, not logic.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: ResponseEntity is a runtime object. You build it inside the method and can set any status code you want based on what actually happened — resource found, resource missing, business rule failed.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) on a DELETE method that always returns 204 — it's cleaner than wrapping the void return in a ResponseEntity. Use ResponseEntity when you might return 200 or 404, or when you need to set a Location header.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: sharp edge: If a method returns ResponseEntity, any @ResponseStatus annotation on that method is completely ignored. Spring uses the status from the ResponseEntity object. You can't combine both.

cap: Rule of thumb: if you already know at compile time what status to return, use @ResponseStatus. If the status depends on logic, use ResponseEntity.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: List endpoints that return all records with no limit are a ticking time bomb — pagination is not optional in production.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Collection endpoints should return paginated data. Spring Data's Page<T> return type gives you the data slice plus metadata: total elements, total pages, and current page number. Clients know exactly how many pages exist and can request the next one.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Single-object endpoints should handle the not-found case explicitly. Return the object with 200 if found, return 404 if not. The Optional map pattern with ResponseEntity is the clean way to express this.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Page<T>: paginates the data and includes count metadata — good for list endpoints.
List<T>: fine only if the dataset is guaranteed to be small — like a fixed enum list.
Empty list: return 200 with empty array [] — not 404. 404 means the collection doesn't exist.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: production trap: Calling userRepository.findAll() with no pagination in a controller that serves production traffic will eventually cause an OutOfMemoryError when the table has millions of rows. Always add page and size parameters with sensible defaults. Validate the size parameter with @Max to cap it.

cap: Use lighter response DTOs for list endpoints — fewer fields means smaller payloads. Reserve the full detail DTO for single-item endpoints.
